newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright to bring NATO sweetners to Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Albright to bring NATO sweetners to Moscow.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright comes to Russia on Thursday with a package of measures designed to woo Moscow into dropping its objections to NATO expansion.
Albright, on her first trip abroad since taking up the job, has been to Brussels and London to try to foster a united front in the western alliance's tricky negotiations with Russia.
She is expected to outline several major new initiatives in her talks in Moscow, which insists that allowing former Warsaw Pact countries to join NATO threatens Russia's security.

The sweetners include the offer of a joint NATO-Russia military brigade, mainly to be used in peacekeeping, and a NATO-Russia meeting with potential new alliance members before July, when the first invitations are due to go out.
Albright is also expected to explain sweeping changes to a landmark arms control treaty agreed by NATO allies on Wednesday in another bid to win Moscow round.

The changes to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty take account of several Russian objections to existing ceilings on arsenals, which Moscow says are rooted in the Cold War and put it at a disadvantage.

But despite the flurry of efforts to address Russia's concerns, Albright faces a tough task in Moscow, which suspects that her Eastern European background has coloured her approach to Russia, something she firmly denies.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel who blazed this week's diplomatic trail to Moscow, said on Wednesday he had found no softening in the Russian stance.

"Everyone I have met has shown resistance to NATO enlargement," Kinkel said after meetings with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and a telephone conversation with President Boris Yeltsin.

Rodionov said in turn that he had heard no new arguments in favour of expanding the alliance from Kinkel. "They simply tried to convince us once again that it is good for Russia and for Europe," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini arrived in Moscow on Wednesday evening to take up the diplomatic baton with talks on European security and the settlement of crisis situations.
Albright hopes that her two-day visit to Moscow will bring a breakthrough in relations in time for a summit between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next month.
Moscow has yet to comment on the new proposals she will bring although officials have said they are interested in hearing more about them from her.
But domestic political considerations mean that however they view Albright's offers, they are likely to keep up the pressure on NATO for more concessions.
Yeltsin, under fire from his political opponents over ill health, has been at pains to present a tough line over NATO expansion to bolster his image as a strong and capable leader.
But as usual, it was opposition communists and nationalists who came up with the strongest rhetoric.
"The West, as always, is cheating Orthodox Christians," said Albert Makashov, a communist retired general who serves on the lower house of parliament's defence committee.
